title: The history of understanding taste
tagline: From Aristotle and the six rasas of Ayurveda to a myth-making tongue map, the discovery of umami, and receptors for every taste.
intro: People have argued about how many tastes there are for over 2,000 years. For most of that time taste was a matter of philosophy and cooking. Microscopes found the taste buds, careful tests found (and a misreading invented) a tongue map, and a Japanese chemist found a taste Europe had missed. In the last 30 years, genetics revealed the receptor for each of the five tastes, and showed that chilli heat is really a pain and heat sensor at work.

eras.name: Naming the tastes
eras.summary: Philosophers and physicians in Greece and India sort tastes into short lists, including some, like pungent and astringent, that science now calls touch.

eras.name: Buds, maps and myths
eras.summary: Microscopes reveal the taste buds; a study of the tongue edge is misread into the famous tongue map, then tested and found wrong.

eras.name: Umami, chillies and genes
eras.summary: A fifth taste is found in seaweed broth, chilli heat gets a scale, and some people turn out to be blind to a bitter chemical.

eras.name: A receptor for every taste
eras.summary: Genetics finds the sensors: T1Rs for sweet and umami, T2Rs for bitter, ENaC for salt, OTOP1 for sour, and TRP channels for heat and cold.

eras.name: Records, a pandemic and a Nobel
eras.summary: Chilli breeders chase heat records, COVID-19 shows the world how flavour depends on smell, and the heat sensor wins a Nobel Prize.

events.title: Aristotle lists the tastes
events.text: In his book On the Soul, Aristotle wrote that the two basic tastes are sweet and bitter. Between them he placed oily, salty, pungent, harsh (astringent) and sour, a list of seven or eight flavours.
events.why: It was one of the first attempts to sort tastes into a short list of basics, an idea still used today.

events.date: c. 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE
events.title: Ayurveda names six rasas
events.who: The Charaka Samhita (compiled by physicians in the tradition of Agnivesha and Charaka)
events.text: The Charaka Samhita, a founding text of Ayurveda, describes six rasas, or tastes: madhura (sweet), amla (sour), lavana (salty), katu (pungent), tikta (bitter) and kashaya (astringent). A healthy diet, it says, balances all six. Its date is uncertain; it was revised over several centuries.
events.why: Its six tastes include pungent and astringent, which science now files under touch and pain rather than taste, as this box shows.

events.title: Taste buds are discovered
events.text: Working separately, the Swedish anatomist Christian Lovén and the German anatomist Gustav Schwalbe looked at the tongue under the microscope and found small onion-shaped clusters of cells, which they called taste bulbs or taste goblets.
events.why: It showed that taste is sensed by special groups of cells, not by the whole tongue surface.

events.title: Hänig measures the edge of the tongue
events.text: In a paper called "On the psychophysics of the sense of taste", Hänig dripped sweet, sour, salty and bitter solutions on spots around the edge of people's tongues and found the weakest strength each could notice. The differences between spots were small.
events.why: His careful data were later misread as a tongue map, one of the most famous myths in science teaching.

events.title: Ikeda finds umami in kombu
events.text: The chemist Kikunae Ikeda wondered why kombu seaweed broth (dashi) tasted so savoury. He boiled down large amounts of kombu and extracted glutamic acid, whose salts gave the taste. He named it umami, from the Japanese for "delicious".
events.why: It was the first scientific claim for a fifth basic taste, though the West took most of a century to accept it.

events.title: MSG goes on sale
events.text: Ikeda patented a way to make monosodium glutamate (MSG) and teamed up with the businessman Saburosuke Suzuki to sell it as a seasoning called Ajinomoto, "essence of taste".
events.why: It turned a taste discovery into one of the world's most widely used food ingredients.

events.title: Scoville measures chilli heat
events.text: The pharmacist Wilbur Scoville, working for the drug company Parke-Davis, soaked dried chillies in alcohol, then diluted the extract with sugar water until a panel of tasters could no longer feel the heat. The number of dilutions became the Scoville heat unit.
events.why: It gave the world a scale for chilli heat, still used today, though labs now measure capsaicin with machines.

events.title: The chemical some people cannot taste
events.text: Fox was pouring a powder called PTC when some of it blew into the air. His colleague C. R. Noller complained it was very bitter; Fox, standing closer, tasted nothing. Testing others showed that people differ: roughly a third of people worldwide cannot taste it.
events.why: It was the first clear sign that taste is partly in our genes. The gene, TAS2R38, a bitter receptor, was found in 2003.

events.title: A graph without units starts a myth
events.text: In his history of the psychology of the senses, Boring redrew Hänig's 1901 results as a graph of how sensitive each part of the tongue edge was, with no numbers on the scale. Readers took the peaks to mean each taste lived in only one area, and a tongue map spread into textbooks.
events.why: It shows how a small misreading can travel for decades.

events.title: Taste cells are always being replaced
events.text: By labelling new cells in rats, Beidler and Smallman showed that taste-bud cells are constantly replaced, living about ten days on average before new ones take their place.
events.why: It explains why taste usually recovers after a burn from hot food or drink.

events.title: The tongue map is tested and fails
events.text: Collings repeated the tests on many spots of the tongue and found that all four tastes then known could be sensed everywhere with taste buds. The weakest noticeable strength differed a little from place to place, but no area was blind to any taste.
events.why: It was the scientific end of the tongue map, even if school books kept it for years.

events.title: Umami becomes a scientific word
events.text: Researchers from many countries met in Hawaii for the first international meeting on umami. Shizuko Yamaguchi showed with careful taste tests that umami could not be made by mixing the other four tastes, and "umami" was adopted as the scientific name for the taste of glutamate.
events.why: It put umami on the world's scientific map, though its receptor was still unknown.

events.title: Supertasters
events.text: Bartoshuk's team found that people fall into three groups for the bitter chemical PROP: non-tasters, medium tasters and "supertasters", who find it intensely bitter and tend to have more fungiform papillae. In their samples, about a quarter of people were supertasters.
events.why: It showed that people really do live in different taste worlds.

events.title: The capsaicin receptor is found
events.where: University of California, San Francisco, USA
events.text: Julius's team searched through thousands of genes for one that made cells respond to capsaicin. They found TRPV1, a channel that also opens at painful heat above about 43 °C.
events.why: It explained why chilli feels hot, and opened the science of how we sense temperature.

events.title: The first taste receptor genes
events.who: Mark Hoon, Nicholas Ryba, Charles Zuker and colleagues
events.where: NIH and University of California, San Diego, USA
events.text: The team found two genes for receptors made only in taste cells, later named T1R1 and T1R2. It took two more years to learn what they detect.
events.why: It was the first step to naming the molecules behind each taste.

events.title: A family of bitter receptors
events.who: Several teams, including Zuker and Ryba, and Linda Buck
events.text: Three papers described the T2Rs, a family of about 25 bitter receptors in humans. Many bitter cells carry several kinds, so one cell can warn of many different poisons. The same year, a team in Miami proposed a glutamate receptor for umami.
events.why: It showed why bitter is so sensitive: it is a warning system built to catch thousands of chemicals.

events.title: Sweet and umami receptors are pinned down
events.who: Greg Nelson, Charles Zuker, Nicholas Ryba and others
events.text: Teams found a third gene, T1R3, and showed that T1R2 + T1R3 together make the sweet receptor (2001), while T1R1 + T1R3 make the umami receptor for glutamate (2002).
events.why: Umami finally had a receptor of its own, and its place as the fifth basic taste was settled.

events.title: The cold and menthol sensor
events.who: David Julius's and Ardem Patapoutian's labs
events.where: San Francisco and La Jolla, USA
events.text: Two teams independently found TRPM8, a channel on nerve endings that opens with cool temperatures and with menthol from mint.
events.why: It explained why mint feels cold even when it is not.

events.title: The first million-Scoville chilli
events.where: New Mexico State University, USA, with seeds from north-east India
events.text: Guinness World Records certified the bhut jolokia, the "ghost pepper" grown in Assam and nearby states, as the world's hottest chilli, after lab tests measured 1,001,304 Scoville heat units.
events.why: It was the first chilli certified above a million SHU, nearly double the previous record holder.

events.title: The salt channel
events.who: Jayaram Chandrashekar, Charles Zuker, Nicholas Ryba and colleagues
events.text: Mice without the sodium channel ENaC in their taste cells lost their liking for low salt. So ENaC is the sensor for pleasant saltiness, while very salty food also triggers bitter and sour cells.
events.why: It explained why a little salt tastes good and a lot tastes bad.

events.title: The Carolina Reaper
events.text: Guinness World Records confirmed the Carolina Reaper, a cross-bred chilli, as the hottest, at an average of 1,569,300 Scoville heat units; a 2017 re-test put it at 1,641,183.
events.why: Breeders were now deliberately crossing chillies to push the heat higher.

events.title: Is fat a sixth taste?
events.who: Cordelia Running, Bruce Craig and Richard Mattes
events.text: Taste tests suggested that fatty acids have a taste of their own, which the team proposed calling "oleogustus". Earlier work had found fat-sensing receptors such as CD36 on taste cells. Scientists still debate it, along with "kokumi", a richness linked to a calcium-sensing receptor.
events.why: The list of basic tastes may not be finished.

events.title: The sour receptor at last
events.who: Emily Liman's lab; Charles Zuker's lab
events.where: Los Angeles and New York, USA
events.text: Sour was the last basic taste without a known receptor. In 2018 Liman's team showed that OTOP1, a channel that lets protons in, is found in sour cells. In 2019 her lab and Zuker's showed that mice without it barely sense sour.
events.why: It completed the set: each of the five tastes now has a known sensor.

events.title: Losing taste and smell to COVID-19
events.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, sudden loss of smell, and with it much of the sense of taste, became one of the best-known symptoms. Health services such as the UK's NHS and the US CDC added it to their symptom lists in 2020.
events.why: Millions of people learned how much of flavour depends on smell, and research into smell loss grew fast.

events.title: A Nobel Prize for heat and touch
events.text: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Julius, for finding TRPV1 with capsaicin, and to Patapoutian, for finding the touch sensors PIEZO1 and PIEZO2. Both also found TRPM8, the cold sensor.
events.why: The science behind chilli heat and minty cool reached the top of medicine.

events.title: Pepper X
events.text: Guinness World Records named Pepper X, bred by the grower of the Carolina Reaper over a decade, the hottest chilli, at an average of 2,693,000 Scoville heat units.
events.why: Chilli breeding keeps pushing a plant's defence chemical to extremes.

people.name: Aristotle
people.note: Made one of the first lists of basic tastes, with sweet and bitter as the extremes.

people.name: Kikunae Ikeda
people.note: Found glutamate in kombu broth and named its taste umami.

people.name: Wilbur Scoville
people.note: Invented the dilution test that still gives chilli heat its units.

people.name: Arthur L. Fox
people.note: Discovered by accident that some people cannot taste the bitter chemical PTC.

people.name: Virginia B. Collings
people.note: Tested the tongue map in 1974 and showed that every area with taste buds senses every taste.

people.name: Linda Bartoshuk
people.note: Found supertasters and showed how differently people experience taste.

people.name: Charles Zuker and Nicholas Ryba
people.from: Chile and the UK, working in the USA
people.note: Their labs found or pinned down receptors for sweet, umami, bitter, salt and sour.

people.name: Emily Liman
people.note: Her lab identified OTOP1, the proton channel behind sour taste.

people.name: David Julius
people.note: Used capsaicin to find TRPV1, the heat sensor; Nobel Prize 2021.

people.name: Ardem Patapoutian
people.note: Found the touch sensors PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 and co-discovered the cold sensor TRPM8; Nobel Prize 2021.

series.title: The hottest chilli on record
series.caption: Guinness-certified record holders: from the first million-SHU chilli in 2007, breeders have pushed the heat up by about two and a half times.

points.label: Trinidad Scorpion Butch T (Australia): 1,463,700 SHU, after the Naga Viper briefly held 1,382,118

facts: The tongue map, with sweet on the tip and bitter at the back, is a myth: every part with taste buds tastes all five.
You can notice bitter quinine at a strength over 1,000 times weaker than the weakest sugar you can notice.
Chilli heat is not a taste: capsaicin opens TRPV1, the same sensor that warns of burning heat above about 43 °C.
Your taste cells are replaced about every ten days, some after a few weeks.
Ayurveda counted six tastes about 2,000 years ago; two of them, pungent and astringent, are now known to be touch and pain rather than taste.
